claims.text: Rapid cooling of a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy creates a metastable microstructure rich in dispersed Mg-bearing phases.
Post-processing thermal exposure transforms the metastable Mg-bearing phases into stable intermetallic compounds.
The intermetallic compounds formed during thermal exposure are finely distributed.
The intermetallic compounds formed during thermal exposure preferentially segregate to grain boundaries.
The phase transformation promotes formation of a protective MgO scale during high-temperature oxidation.
The transformed microstructural heterogeneities alter localized electrochemical sites.
The initial rapidly solidified alloy contains a mixed solid solution.
Rapid solidification traps Mg in metastable states.
Grain-boundary accumulation of Mg enhances MgO formation during high-temperature exposure.
The MgO scale retards high-temperature oxidation.
Intermetallic and compositional heterogeneities modify local galvanic coupling in corrosive environments.
Relative to a near-equilibrium processed alloy, the non-equilibrium alloy will exhibit a slower high-temperature oxidation rate.
Relative to a near-equilibrium processed alloy, the non-equilibrium alloy will exhibit altered corrosion rates.
The corrosion change may include an increase in localized corrosion caused by changed microgalvanic activity.
Slow near-equilibrium cooling produces a stable phase distribution without pronounced metastable phase evolution.
Slow near-equilibrium cooling does not produce significant grain-boundary Mg segregation.
The proposed comparison is restricted to alloys with density below 6 g/cm3.
The hypothesis applies to Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys prone to forming both solid solutions and intermetallic compounds.
